title: Wave properties — frequency, wavelength, amplitude
examTip: v = fλ is the key equation. Speed is in m/s, frequency in Hz and wavelength in metres. Always check units before substituting.
introTips: Waves transfer energy from place to place without transferring matter. The medium itself just oscillates.
Transverse and longitudinal waves both carry energy. But they do it in very different ways.
The wave equation v = fλ connects three things you can measure. Learn to rearrange it both ways.
Diffraction is why you can hear someone around a corner, even though you can't see them.
Period and frequency are reciprocals. Double the frequency and you halve the period.
intro: Every time you hear music, feel the sun's warmth or send a text message, waves are doing the work. Waves are how energy moves through space. Engineers use wave properties to design Wi-Fi networks, ultrasound scanners and noise-cancelling headphones. A wave might be a ripple on a pond, sound from a speaker or light from your phone screen. The same few properties describe them all: frequency, wavelength, amplitude and speed. Get comfortable with these, and the rest of the waves topic clicks into place.

keyPoints.heading: Transverse and longitudinal waves
keyPoints.content: All waves transfer energy without transferring matter. There are two types. Transverse waves: the oscillation (vibration) is perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of travel. Examples are light, all electromagnetic waves, water waves and waves on a string. Longitudinal waves: the oscillation is parallel to the direction of travel, along the same line. This makes compressions (particles pushed together) and rarefactions (particles pulled apart). Sound is the key example. A useful memory check: transverse = 'T' shape. The oscillation is at right angles to the travel, like a 'T'. Longitudinal = 'L' for 'along'. The oscillation is along the same line.
writeBullets: Transverse wave — oscillation perpendicular to the direction of travel (for example, light, water, EM waves)
Longitudinal wave — oscillation parallel to the direction of travel (for example, sound)
Compression — a region where particles are pushed close together in a longitudinal wave
Rarefaction — a region where particles are spread apart in a longitudinal wave
All waves transfer energy but not matter. The medium oscillates in place

keyTerms.def: A wave where oscillation is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer — e.g. light, water waves
A wave where oscillation is parallel to the direction of energy transfer — e.g. sound
A region of high pressure in a longitudinal wave where particles are pushed together
A region of low pressure in a longitudinal wave where particles are spread apart

keyPoints.memTip: Transverse = T-shape (at right angles). Longitudinal = along the line.
keyPoints.tutor_note: People often say sound is transverse. Remember the 'along the same line' definition. Link it to the compression and rarefaction diagram.

keyPoints.heading: Amplitude, wavelength, frequency, and period
keyPoints.content: Amplitude (A): the maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its rest (equilibrium) position. A bigger amplitude = more energy carried by the wave. It is measured in metres. Wavelength (λ): the distance between two neighbouring points that are in phase. For example, crest to crest, or trough to trough. It is measured in metres. Frequency (f): the number of complete waves passing a point per second. It is measured in hertz (Hz). 1 Hz = 1 wave per second. Period (T): the time for one complete wave to pass a point. It is measured in seconds (s). Period and frequency are reciprocals: T = 1/f and f = 1/T. Doubling the frequency halves the period.
writeBullets: Amplitude — the maximum displacement from the rest position. Bigger amplitude = more energy
Wavelength (λ) — the distance from one crest to the next (or trough to trough). Unit: metres
Frequency (f) — the number of complete waves per second. Unit: hertz (Hz)
Period (T) — the time for one complete wave. Unit: seconds (s)
T = 1/f. Period and frequency are reciprocals of each other

keyTerms.def: Maximum displacement of a wave from its equilibrium (rest) position; larger amplitude means more energy
Distance between two successive points in phase, e.g. crest to crest; measured in metres
Number of complete wave cycles passing a point per second; measured in hertz (Hz)
Time for one complete wave cycle; T = 1/f; measured in seconds

keyPoints.memTip: AWFP: Amplitude, Wavelength, Frequency, Period. These four properties are all linked by T = 1/f and v = fλ.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Amplitude and wavelength are often mixed up on wave diagrams. Practise labelling diagrams. Amplitude is measured vertically, and wavelength horizontally.

keyPoints.heading: The wave equation: v = fλ
keyPoints.content: The wave equation links the speed, frequency and wavelength of any wave: v = fλ. Here v = wave speed (m/s), f = frequency (Hz) and λ = wavelength (m). Rearrangements: f = v/λ and λ = v/f. Worked example 1: a wave has frequency 200 Hz and wavelength 1.5 m. Speed = 200 × 1.5 = 300 m/s. Worked example 2: a wave travels at 340 m/s with wavelength 0.17 m. Frequency = 340 ÷ 0.17 = 2000 Hz. Worked example 3: an EM wave travels at 3×10⁸ m/s with frequency 1×10⁹ Hz. Wavelength = 3×10⁸ ÷ 1×10⁹ = 0.3 m. The wave equation applies to ALL wave types: sound, light, water and seismic waves.
writeBullets: Wave equation: v = fλ (speed = frequency × wavelength)
Rearrangement: f = v ÷ λ (frequency = speed ÷ wavelength)
Rearrangement: λ = v ÷ f (wavelength = speed ÷ frequency)
Units: v in m/s, f in Hz, λ in m. Always check before substituting
Applies to all waves: sound, light, water, seismic waves

keyTerms.def: v = fλ; wave speed (m/s) = frequency (Hz) × wavelength (m)
How fast the wave travels through the medium; measured in m/s

keyPoints.memTip: v = fλ: 'very fast lambda'. Speed = frequency × wavelength. Cover what you want to find with your finger. Then multiply or divide the other two.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Write the formula, substitute values with units, then calculate. Method marks are available even if the final figure is wrong.

keyPoints.heading: Reflection, refraction, and diffraction
keyPoints.content: Reflection: waves bounce off a surface. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Both are measured from the normal, a line at right angles to the surface. The wave speed and frequency do not change. Refraction: when a wave crosses a boundary between two media, its speed changes. If it hits at an angle, its direction changes too. A wave that slows down bends toward the normal. A wave that speeds up bends away from the normal. The frequency stays the same, but the wavelength changes. Diffraction: waves spread out as they pass through a gap or around an obstacle. Diffraction is strongest when the gap size is similar to the wavelength. Compared with the wavelength, a narrow gap diffracts more than a wide one. This is why long-wavelength radio waves diffract around hills, but short-wavelength light does not.
writeBullets: Reflection — waves bounce off a surface. Angle of incidence = angle of reflection (from the normal)
Refraction — wave speed changes at a boundary. The direction changes if it hits at an angle
Slows down at a boundary → bends toward the normal. Speeds up → bends away from the normal
Diffraction — waves spread around obstacles or through gaps
Most diffraction when gap ≈ wavelength. A wider gap = less diffraction (compared with the wavelength)

keyTerms.def: Wave bounces off a surface; angle of incidence = angle of reflection, both from the normal
Change in wave speed at a boundary causing a change in direction (frequency unchanged)
Spreading of waves around an obstacle or through a gap; greatest when gap ≈ wavelength
An imaginary line perpendicular to a surface, used as the reference for measuring angles of incidence and reflection

keyPoints.memTip: Refraction: waves slow → bend toward the normal, like a car wheel catching mud on one side. Diffraction is strongest when gap ≈ wavelength.
keyPoints.tutor_note: People often say diffraction happens 'when the gap is smaller than the wavelength'. The correct phrase is 'similar to the wavelength'. Also describe what happens to the shape of the wavefronts.

0.question: Sound waves are described as longitudinal. What does this mean?
options: The particles oscillate parallel to (along) the direction the wave travels
The particles oscillate perpendicular to the direction the wave travels
The wave can travel through a vacuum
The wave travels faster than light
0.correctFeedback: Correct! In a longitudinal wave, particles oscillate along the same direction as the wave travels. This makes compressions and rarefactions.
0.wrongFeedback: Longitudinal means 'along the line'. Particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel. In transverse waves, like light and water waves, the oscillation is perpendicular to the travel.

1.question: A wave has a frequency of 500 Hz and travels at 340 m/s. What is its wavelength?
1.correctFeedback: Correct! λ = v ÷ f = 340 ÷ 500 = 0.68 m. When you want the wavelength, always rearrange v = fλ to λ = v/f.
1.wrongFeedback: Use λ = v ÷ f = 340 ÷ 500 = 0.68 m. Make sure you divide speed by frequency. Don't multiply.

3.question: A wave passes through a gap. When does it diffract (spread out) most?
options: The gap width is similar to the wavelength of the wave
The gap is much wider than the wavelength
The frequency of the wave is very high
The wave travels through a vacuum
3.correctFeedback: Exactly right! Diffraction is strongest when the gap size is about equal to the wavelength. A much wider gap gives much less spreading.
3.wrongFeedback: Diffraction is strongest when gap size ≈ wavelength. If the gap is much wider than the wavelength, the wave passes through with very little spreading.

commonMistakes: Mixing up amplitude and wavelength on a wave diagram. Amplitude is the vertical distance from rest to crest. Wavelength is the horizontal distance from crest to crest.
Saying diffraction only happens when the gap is smaller than the wavelength. It is strongest when gap ≈ wavelength. It still happens at other sizes, but much less.
Forgetting to check units before using v = fλ. Frequency must be in Hz and wavelength in metres to get speed in m/s.
Saying that refraction changes a wave's frequency. Refraction changes the speed and wavelength, but the frequency stays constant.
Describing sound as a transverse wave. Sound is longitudinal. Its particles oscillate parallel to the direction of travel.
examTips: v = fλ: always write the formula first, then substitute with units. Method marks count, even if you make an arithmetic slip.
For reflection and refraction questions, always measure angles from the normal. Never measure from the surface itself.
When explaining diffraction, say 'the gap width is similar to the wavelength'. Vague answers like 'the gap is small' will not get full marks.
In longitudinal vs transverse questions, give an example of each: sound (longitudinal), and light or EM waves (transverse).
Period and frequency are linked: T = 1/f. If you know one, you can always find the other.
revisionCardBullets: Transverse wave — oscillation perpendicular to the direction of travel (for example, light, EM waves, water)
Longitudinal wave — oscillation parallel to the direction of travel (for example, sound). Has compressions and rarefactions
Amplitude — the maximum displacement from rest. Bigger = more energy
Wavelength (λ) — the distance from crest to crest. Unit: metres
Frequency (f) — waves per second. Unit: Hz
Period (T) — the time for one wave. T = 1/f. Unit: seconds
Wave equation: v = fλ. It rearranges to f = v/λ and λ = v/f
Reflection — angle of incidence = angle of reflection (from the normal). Speed unchanged
Refraction — speed changes at a boundary. Slows → bends toward the normal
Diffraction — waves spread through gaps. Strongest when gap ≈ wavelength
Frequency unchanged by reflection or refraction
